title: Open reduction and internal fixation of the ankle
subtitle: Lateral malleolus plate and syndesmosis fixation for an unstable ankle fracture

sources.title: BOAST: The management of ankle fractures
Close contact casting vs surgery for initial treatment of unstable ankle fractures in older adults: a randomized clinical trial

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Venous thromboembolism in over 16s: reducing the risk of hospital-acquired deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism (NG89)

indications: Unstable ankle fractures: bimalleolar and trimalleolar fractures, and lateral malleolus fractures with talar shift or medial injury (deltoid ligament).
Fractures with syndesmotic injury (often Weber C, or Maisonneuve patterns).
Fractures that cannot be held reduced in a cast, or open fractures after debridement.
In older adults with unstable fractures, close contact casting is a reasonable alternative with similar function at 6 months (AIM trial); discuss both options.
contraindications: Swollen or blistered skin over the incision: delay surgery until the swelling settles and stabilise the ankle in a cast or spanning external fixator meanwhile.
Severe peripheral arterial disease or uncontrolled diabetes with poor skin: weigh fixation against casting with the patient.
Stable isolated lateral malleolus fractures with no talar shift: treat without surgery.
preparation: Reduce a dislocated or subluxed ankle immediately in the emergency department and splint, with neurovascular checks and radiographs after reduction (BOAST).
Anteroposterior, mortise and lateral radiographs; full-length tibia and fibula views if a proximal fibular fracture is suspected; CT for posterior malleolar or complex patterns.
Assess diabetes, neuropathy, smoking and peripheral pulses; plan longer protection if neuropathy is present.

Consent risks to discuss: infection, wound breakdown, nerve injury (superficial peroneal, sural, saphenous), malreduction, loss of fixation, prominent metalwork needing removal, venous thromboembolism, stiffness, post-traumatic arthritis, complex regional pain syndrome, and the non-operative alternative.
positioning: Supine with a sandbag under the ipsilateral buttock to internally rotate the leg, or lateral for a posterior approach.
Thigh tourniquet; heel on a padded support so the C-arm can obtain true mortise and lateral views.
equipment: Small fragment set with one-third tubular and anatomical distal fibular plates, lag and locking screws.
Pointed reduction clamps, K-wires, bone hook, syndesmotic screws or suture-button devices.
Image intensifier with a radiolucent table extension.
anatomy: The superficial peroneal nerve pierces the deep fascia in the distal leg and crosses anterior to the fibula at a variable level, so it is at risk in the proximal wound.
The syndesmosis comprises the anterior and posterior inferior tibiofibular ligaments and the interosseous ligament; the fibula sits in the incisura of the tibia.
The deltoid ligament is the main medial stabiliser; its rupture with a lateral malleolus fracture makes the injury unstable even without a medial fracture.
Fibular length and rotation determine the position of the talus in the mortise.
criticalSafety: Operate when the soft tissues allow, not when the list allows.
Restore fibular length and rotation before judging the syndesmosis.
Always test the syndesmosis after fixation and confirm congruent mortise on the final images.
structuresAtRisk: Long saphenous vein and saphenous nerve
Anterior tibial vessels and deep peroneal nerve during syndesmotic drilling
commonErrors: Syndesmotic malreduction from a misdirected clamp.
Distal screws in the lateral malleolus entering the joint.
complications: Wound breakdown and infection, more frequent in diabetes, smoking and older patients.
Malreduction, loss of fixation, syndesmotic diastasis.
Venous thromboembolism, complex regional pain syndrome, stiffness and post-traumatic arthritis.
postop: Elevation, backslab or boot, and a wound check before definitive cast or boot.
Weight bearing per the fixation and the surgeon's instruction; many stable constructs allow early protected weight bearing, while syndesmotic fixation and neuropathy may need longer protection.
Thromboprophylaxis assessment for lower-limb immobilisation per NICE NG89.
Clinic review with radiographs; plan for syndesmotic screw removal only if the local protocol requires it.

steps.emphasis: Check the skin and the wrinkle sign before confirming the operation goes ahead today.
Supine with a sandbag under the buttock so the fibula faces up; heel clear of the table for the C-arm.
Confirm a true mortise view (about 15 to 20 degrees of internal rotation) and a true lateral before preparing.
Restore fibular length, rotation and alignment; the talus should sit congruent in the mortise with a normal medial clear space.
For a short oblique Weber B fracture: an interfragmentary lag screw, then a neutralisation plate laterally or an antiglide plate posterolaterally. Avoid long distal screws entering the joint.
Mortise and lateral: congruent joint, equal medial clear space, fibular length restored, no intra-articular screws.
If the skin is not ready or the reduction cannot be held, stabilise with a spanning external fixator and return when the soft tissues allow.
Tension-free closure with careful handling of thin skin over the plate.
State the weight-bearing instruction and the length of protection explicitly.

step.ankle.lateral-approach.title: Lateral approach to the distal fibula
step.ankle.lateral-approach.why: The fibula is subcutaneous, so the approach is simple, but the superficial peroneal nerve crosses from posterior to anterior in the distal leg at a variable level and the skin over the fibula tolerates little retraction or a prominent plate.
how: Incise along the posterior border of the fibula (or directly lateral, according to the planned plate position), centred on the fracture.
Before deepening proximally, look for the superficial peroneal nerve crossing anteriorly in the subcutaneous tissue and protect it.
Incise periosteum only along the line needed to see the fracture edges; keep full-thickness skin flaps and avoid heavy retraction.
structuresAtRisk: Sural nerve and short saphenous vein (posterior incision)
pitfalls: Cutting the superficial peroneal nerve in the proximal part of the wound.
Undermining thin flaps that later break down over the plate.

step.ankle.medial-malleolus.title: Medial malleolus reduction and fixation
step.ankle.medial-malleolus.why: A displaced medial malleolar fracture leaves the talus unstable and the joint incongruent. Periosteum folded into the fracture is the usual reason it will not reduce or heal.
how: Anteromedial incision over the fracture, protecting the long saphenous vein and saphenous nerve.
Clear interposed periosteum, inspect the anteromedial joint surface and the talar dome, and reduce with a pointed clamp or a K-wire joystick.
Fix with two partially threaded cancellous screws perpendicular to the fracture, or a tension band or plate for small or vertical fragments.
Screen to confirm the screws do not enter the joint.
structuresAtRisk: Long saphenous vein and saphenous nerve
Tibialis posterior tendon behind the malleolus
pitfalls: Accepting a gap with interposed periosteum.
Screws angled into the joint or through the posterior cortex into tibialis posterior.

step.ankle.syndesmosis.title: Syndesmosis: test, reduce and fix
step.ankle.syndesmosis.why: An unstable syndesmosis left unfixed lets the talus shift, but a syndesmosis fixed in a malreduced position is common and harms outcome as much. Testing, then accurate reduction into the incisura, both matter.
how: After fibular fixation, stress the syndesmosis: a lateral pull on the fibula with a bone hook, and an external rotation stress under fluoroscopy. Look for widening of the medial clear space and tibiofibular clear space.

If unstable, reduce the fibula into the incisura under direct vision or fluoroscopy, checking fibular length and rotation; use a clamp with moderate force, aligned with the axis of the incisura, to avoid over-compression and malreduction.
Fix with syndesmotic screws or a suture-button device placed above the joint, parallel to the plafond and angled from posterolateral to anteromedial.
Compare with the uninjured ankle's images or use intra-operative assessment where the reduction is uncertain; open and reduce directly if in doubt.
structuresAtRisk: Anterior tibial vessels and deep peroneal nerve (anteromedial drill exit)
Long saphenous vein and nerve (medial drill exit)
pitfalls: Clamp placed obliquely, pushing the fibula anterior or posterior in the incisura.
Not testing the syndesmosis because the fibula fracture looked low.
Fixing a fibula left short or externally rotated.
